paragraphs: The paper studies how to approximate a population distribution when drawing random samples from it is impossible. Instead, the learner has an existing dataset and can ask an oracle how much probability the target distribution assigns to examples similar to a selected example. Database counts and search-result counts illustrate the kind of access the authors have in mind.

The proposed algorithm repeatedly chooses an example, requests its weight information, and adjusts the dataset’s weights. Its selection strategy draws inspiration from upper confidence bounds in bandit learning. A new discrepancy estimator and a greedy update procedure help guide this interaction, so that a limited number of queries can support a useful reweighting.

The theoretical guarantee measures total variation distance relative to the best reweighting achievable with the available dataset. That comparison matters: the result concerns how effectively the algorithm uses its available examples. Experiments also show advantages over several baselines, supporting the value of actively choosing which weight queries to make.
icml-2021-approximating-a-distribution-u.tldr: An interactive algorithm approximates a target distribution by selectively querying population weights and reweighting an existing dataset.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from previously collected data, avoiding potentially unsafe or impractical exploration. But a policy can encounter different physical dynamics when deployed. The paper highlights this transfer problem: existing methods can lose up to 90% of their performance when the environment’s dynamics change, even though training addressed differences between the data-collection policy and the learned policy.

Augmented World Models introduces simple transformations of a learned dynamics model to represent possible changes in a robot’s physical properties. The policy trains with these variations and receives the sampled transformation as context. This gives it information about which version of the dynamics it is currently facing, allowing its behavior to depend on that variation.

At test time, the method learns context through self-supervision by approximating the transformation corresponding to the new environment. Evaluation across more than 100 changed-dynamics settings shows significant improvements to a recent baseline’s zero-shot generalization. The approach often produces successful policies in settings where that baseline fails.
icml-2021-augmented-world-models-facilit.tldr: Augmenting a learned world model and conditioning policies on those changes improves transfer to unfamiliar dynamics from a single offline environment.

paragraphs: This paper studies decentralized learning in matching markets where two sides must be paired, but only one side receives bandit feedback. The objective is to reduce regret relative to the agent-optimal stable matching. For general markets, the authors obtain O(log^(1+ε)(T)) regret for any positive ε, improving the previous squared-logarithmic rate without requiring advance knowledge of the time horizon.

A stronger result applies to markets satisfying uniqueness consistency, where departing participants do not change the original stable matching. Under this condition, the algorithm achieves the optimal Θ(log(T)) rate. Earlier logarithmic guarantees required the more restrictive serial-dictatorship setting, in which all arms rank the agents in the same order.

The algorithm proceeds in phases and combines globally communicated removal of dominated arms with local removal of arms that produce frequent collisions. These local decisions help resolve deadlocks caused by different arms ranking agents differently. Simulations also show advantages over existing methods, complementing the theoretical improvements for both general and structured markets.
icml-2021-beyond-log-2-t-regret-for-dece.tldr: Decentralized matching algorithms improve regret rates, with optimal logarithmic regret under a stated consistency condition.

paragraphs: Message-passing graph networks are attractive because they scale efficiently on sparse graphs, but their usual expressive power is limited by the first-order Weisfeiler-Lehman test, or 1-WL. This paper investigates whether a different construction of graph convolutions can exceed that limit while keeping the computation spatially localized.

The proposed construction designs convolution supports in the spectral domain using a custom nonlinear function of graph eigenvalues. It then masks those supports with a receptive field that can be arbitrarily large. Under this design, the authors establish expressive power beyond 1-WL. Custom spectral filters also produce different frequency components, allowing the model to learn different relationships between graph signals and their associated properties.

Experiments find performance comparable in expressive power to existing 3-WL models and state-of-the-art results on many downstream tasks. The theoretical claim is specifically stronger-than-1-WL expressiveness; the 3-WL comparison is experimental. The method also addresses the computational, memory, and nonlocal-update drawbacks identified for existing 3-WL-equivalent networks.
icml-2021-breaking-the-limits-of-message.tldr: Custom spectral convolutions make localized message-passing networks provably more expressive than 1-WL and competitive with stronger graph models experimentally.

paragraphs: Generating an action video requires coordinating what happens, where it happens, and when it happens. The paper focuses on a particular gap in existing methods: conditioning a video on several timed actions that may overlap. It introduces Action Graphs as a structured representation of those actions and defines a task of generating a video from that representation.

The proposed model, AG2Vid, separates features describing motion from features describing appearance. It also includes a mechanism for scheduling actions, helping the generated events occur at the appropriate times and in coordination with one another. This organization gives the generator a way to handle multiple action instructions within one video.

Training and evaluation use the CATER and Something-Something V2 datasets. The resulting videos improve on the baselines in visual quality and semantic consistency, meaning their content better matches the specified actions. The model also generates previously unseen combinations of learned actions, demonstrating zero-shot composition of familiar action components.
icml-2021-compositional-video-synthesis-.tldr: AG2Vid uses Action Graphs and action scheduling to generate coordinated videos, including novel combinations of learned actions.

paragraphs: Graph networks can struggle to distinguish information arriving from different directions. The paper connects this lack of direction-sensitive kernels to limited expressiveness and problems such as over-smoothing. It introduces kernels whose directional interpretation is globally consistent across a graph, with directions derived from the graph’s own topology.

The method first defines a vector field over the graph and projects messages associated with individual nodes into that field. This supports directional derivatives and directional smoothing. The authors then use eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian to supply the field, enabling directions to be embedded without supervision. They show that the construction generalizes convolutional networks on n-dimensional grids and has greater discriminative power than standard GNNs relative to 1-WL.

Reported results include relative error reductions of 8% on CIFAR10 graphs and 11% to 32% on ZINC, plus a 1.6% relative precision increase on MolPCBA. These findings support the usefulness of representing directional features, including those relevant to physical and biological problems.
icml-2021-directional-graph-networks-155.tldr: Directional Graph Networks derive consistent directions from graph structure to improve expressive power and benchmark performance.

paragraphs: A classifier can make accurate predictions while assigning probabilities that exaggerate how often it is correct. This paper examines the common explanation that such over-confidence mainly arises because a model has enough parameters to memorize its training data. Its theory shows that over-parametrization is not required for the problem to occur.

The authors prove over-confidence for logistic regression in a realizable, under-parametrized setting: the data follows the assumed logistic model, and there are many more samples than parameters. They extend the finding to well-specified binary classification problems whose activation function is symmetric and concave on its positive part. These conditions identify a broader setting in which confidence can still be systematically too high.

The analysis also demonstrates that over-confidence is not inevitable across activation choices. Another activation, paired with a suitable loss, yields under-confidence at some probability values. Simulations and real-data experiments verify the theory, showing that calibration depends on the learning formulation even when the assumed model correctly describes the data.
icml-2021-dont-just-blame-over-parametri.tldr: Even correctly specified, under-parametrized classifiers can be over-confident, and activation choices can also produce under-confidence.

paragraphs: Training variational autoencoders depends on estimating gradients through random variables. The reparameterization trick makes these estimates more efficient and less variable. Doubly reparameterized gradients take this idea further by applying reparameterization a second time when optimizing variational bounds built from multiple samples. This paper expands where that second application can be used.

The first extension handles hierarchical models with several stochastic layers. Such models introduce additional score-function terms through their hierarchical variational posterior, and the authors show how to treat those terms within the estimator. This brings the method to models whose random variables are organized across multiple levels.

The second extension covers score functions of arbitrary distributions, rather than only the distribution used for sampling. Consequently, the estimator can also apply to prior parameters as well as posterior parameters. The authors show that these generalizations support more effective training of conditional and hierarchical variational autoencoders on image-modeling tasks, broadening the practical reach of the gradient-estimation approach.
icml-2021-generalized-doubly-reparameter.tldr: Two extensions of doubly reparameterized gradients improve training for hierarchical and conditional variational autoencoders.

paragraphs: Finding the largest subgraph shared by two graphs is useful in applications such as drug synthesis and malware detection. The computation is NP-hard, and heuristic solvers can struggle to find good matches for large graph pairs within a limited budget. GLSearch addresses how a solver should spend that search effort.

The method builds on branch and bound, which expands the search by choosing a pair of nodes, one from each input graph. A graph-neural-network-based Deep Q-Network learns which pair to select next. This places learning inside the search procedure, where each decision influences which candidate common subgraphs the algorithm explores.

Experiments on synthetic and real graph pairs show that the learned strategy finds significantly larger common subgraphs than existing solvers given the same computation budget. The practical result is better use of limited search time. The authors also identify potential extensions to other constrained graph-combinatorial problems, presenting that broader applicability as a possibility.
icml-2021-glsearch-maximum-common-subgra.tldr: GLSearch learns node-pair choices inside branch and bound to find larger common subgraphs within the same computation budget.

paragraphs: This paper asks why applying a graph convolution before classification can help when examples have both attributes and graph connections. It studies a specific probabilistic setting: node attributes come from a mixture of Gaussian distributions, and the graph follows a stochastic block model. This setup makes it possible to analyze the contribution of graph information mathematically.

The authors show that graph convolution enlarges the regime in which a linear classifier can separate the data. The improvement has a scaling factor of roughly 1/√D, where D is the expected node degree, relative to using the Gaussian-mixture attributes alone. The result describes how connectivity changes the conditions under which simple classification succeeds.

They also study a linear classifier trained by minimizing cross-entropy after convolution. It generalizes to unseen data with different probabilities of edges within and between classes. This provides a theoretical account of robustness to that particular distribution shift, within the modeled relationship between node attributes and graph structure.
icml-2021-graph-convolution-for-semi-sup.tldr: In a Gaussian-mixture graph model, graph convolution improves linear separability and supports generalization when class-dependent edge probabilities change.

paragraphs: Meta-learning learns a prior from multiple tasks so that a model can adapt quickly to a new task. A common procedure splits each task’s data: one part supports adaptation, and another evaluates the adapted predictor. This paper compares that train-validation procedure with using all per-task data for both steps, focusing theoretically on linear centroid meta-learning.

In the agnostic setting, the expected train-validation objective is minimized at the prior that is optimal for meta-testing. The train-train objective does not generally share this property without additional data structure. When the data is generated by linear models, however, both expected objectives are minimized at the optimal prior.

In that realizable setting, the authors prove that train-train achieves strictly better excess loss, even after optimally tuning regularization and the split ratio. Simulations and real meta-learning tasks also show that train-train can outperform train-validation. The findings make the usefulness of splitting conditional on the relationship between the data and the model.
icml-2021-how-important-is-the-train-val.tldr: Train-validation splitting helps align meta-learning objectives in general, but reusing all task data can be provably better in a realizable linear setting.

paragraphs: Worst-case approximation guarantees describe how well an algorithm must perform across all permitted inputs, but they can understate performance on a particular dataset. For monotone submodular maximization with a limit on the number of selected items, greedy selection has an optimal polynomial-time worst-case guarantee of 1−1/e, approximately 0.63. This paper asks how close a specific solution actually is to optimal.

The authors develop an algorithm that provides an instance-specific approximation assessment for any candidate solution to this problem. Its central tool is a new dual approach. The method constructs a lower bound on the dual objective that can itself be minimized exactly, supporting a comparison between the candidate and the optimum.

Across a wide variety of real datasets and objectives, these assessments show that greedy and other algorithms perform substantially better than their worst-case guarantee suggests. Their approximation levels often exceed 0.9. The contribution therefore helps establish the quality of solutions already found on the instances that matter in practice.
icml-2021-instance-specific-approximatio.tldr: A dual-based method certifies instance-specific solution quality, showing that submodular maximization algorithms often substantially exceed their worst-case guarantee.

paragraphs: Retraining the same neural-network model can change its predictions even when its overall accuracy stays similar. Random initialization and the choice of mini-batches contribute to this disagreement, which the paper calls prediction churn. This matters because aggregate accuracy can hide instability in the predictions made for individual examples.

The authors investigate several baselines for reducing churn and propose training with locally adapted soft labels. Each example’s training label is smoothed according to the labels of neighboring examples. Instead of applying an identical adjustment everywhere, the method lets the local label information determine how the training target is softened.

Across a variety of classification benchmarks and model architectures, this approach often reduces churn more effectively than the baselines while also improving accuracy. The result shows that prediction consistency and accuracy can improve together in the evaluated settings. Its practical contribution is a change to the training targets that directly addresses disagreement between separate training runs.
icml-2021-locally-adaptive-label-smoothi.tldr: Adapting soft training labels to neighboring labels often reduces disagreement between retrained models while improving accuracy.

paragraphs: Independently trained neural networks can reach different parameter settings with similarly low training loss. Earlier findings showed that pairs of such solutions can be connected by one-dimensional paths that keep loss nearly constant. This paper extends that picture by demonstrating multidimensional low-loss structures connecting many independently trained models.

The structures are simplicial complexes: collections of simple geometric pieces that form higher-dimensional regions in parameter space. Their existence means that useful connections among trained solutions can occupy more than a single curve. The authors use this observation to develop an efficient construction procedure aimed at fast ensembling.

The resulting ensembles outperform independently trained deep ensembles in accuracy, calibration, and robustness to dataset shift in the reported evaluation. The procedure needs only a few training epochs to discover a low-loss simplex. Together, these findings connect the geometry of the loss surface to a practical way of building ensembles with better predictive behavior and a short additional training procedure.
icml-2021-loss-surface-simplexes-for-mod.tldr: Multidimensional low-loss connections between trained networks enable fast ensembles with improved accuracy, calibration, and robustness to dataset shift.

paragraphs: Subsampling-based bandit algorithms can avoid specifying a full parametric reward model, but random subsampling and storing all past rewards add complexity. This paper studies a simpler deterministic rule called last-block subsampling. It asks whether this approach can retain strong learning guarantees while reducing the amount of history that must be kept.

The authors prove asymptotic optimality for one-parameter exponential families. They also show that the guarantees survive when memory grows only as a polylogarithmic function of the time horizon. This establishes that, in the analyzed setting, keeping the complete reward history is unnecessary for the stated long-run performance.

The paper then considers changing reward distributions and proposes a variant that subsamples only recent observations. Under the assumption that the number of abrupt changes is known, it achieves optimal regret guarantees. Numerical simulations highlight the approach’s strengths, particularly when changes affect aspects of reward distributions beyond their means. The stationary and changing-environment results each retain their stated assumptions.
icml-2021-on-limited-memory-subsampling-.tldr: Deterministic last-block subsampling retains optimal bandit guarantees with limited memory and supports a variant for abruptly changing rewards.

paragraphs: This paper studies bandit decisions where an option’s quality is measured by Conditional Value at Risk, or CVaR, at a chosen level. The criterion focuses attention on the relevant tail of the reward distribution rather than evaluating options solely by their average rewards. The setting assumes bounded rewards and is motivated by decisions involving physical resources.

The authors introduce Thompson Sampling methods for this objective, extending a line of work that had mainly emphasized upper confidence bounds. B-CVTS handles continuous bounded rewards, while M-CVTS handles multinomial reward distributions. Their theoretical analysis bounds the regret associated with learning which options are best according to CVaR.

The strategies provably match the corresponding asymptotic lower bounds, establishing asymptotic optimality in the studied CVaR bandit setting. This describes their long-run regret behavior. Experiments on synthetic examples and a realistic agricultural-use simulation also illustrate benefits of the Thompson Sampling approach, connecting the theory to risk-sensitive choices in a resource-oriented application.
icml-2021-optimal-thompson-sampling-stra.tldr: Two Thompson Sampling methods achieve asymptotically optimal regret for bounded-reward bandits evaluated using CVaR.

paragraphs: Synthetic controls estimate a counterfactual trajectory: how a unit’s outcomes might have evolved under the alternative being studied. The paper focuses on two restrictions in the existing formulation. Time series are assumed to align across units, and the synthetic control is represented as a linear combination of observed control units.

The proposed alternative works in continuous time and explicitly models the latent counterfactual path using controlled differential equations. Treating the counterfactual as a path gives the method a formulation that can directly accommodate multivariate observations recorded at irregularly aligned times. The target of estimation remains the unobserved trajectory needed for policy analysis.

The model can also be optimized within rich function spaces, expanding the available representations beyond the stated linear-combination formulation. The contribution is therefore a methodological extension of synthetic controls to more flexible temporal and functional settings. Its stated benefit is direct applicability to irregular multivariate time series, addressing the alignment and representation restrictions identified by the authors.
icml-2021-policy-analysis-using-syntheti.tldr: A continuous-time synthetic-control formulation models counterfactual paths for irregularly aligned multivariate time series.

paragraphs: A classifier may rely on correlations that hold in its training environment but fail elsewhere. Predict then Interpolate uses those failures as information. It trains a classifier in one environment and applies it to another, using the distinction between correct and incorrect predictions to investigate which correlations are unstable.

The authors prove that interpolating the distributions of correctly and incorrectly predicted examples can uncover an oracle distribution in which the unstable correlation disappears. The required oracle interpolation coefficients are unavailable. To address that obstacle, the algorithm uses group distributionally robust optimization to minimize the worst-case risk across the possible interpolations.

This turns a theoretical distribution construction into a training objective that does not require knowing the oracle coefficients. Experiments cover both text and image classification. The paper reports improvements over IRM of 23.85% on synthetic environments and 12.41% on natural environments, providing empirical evidence that the approach can learn classifiers that remain robust across environments.
icml-2021-predict-then-interpolate-a-sim.tldr: Predict then Interpolate uses cross-environment prediction errors and robust optimization to learn correlations that remain stable across environments.

paragraphs: An exploration bonus can encourage a reinforcement-learning agent to try actions whose value remains uncertain. Upper confidence bounds provide a principled way to construct such bonuses in tabular and linear settings. This paper addresses the difficulty of carrying that approach into deep reinforcement learning, where those formulations do not directly apply.

Optimistic Bootstrapping and Backward Induction constructs a bonus using a nonparametric bootstrap. The bonus estimates epistemic uncertainty for state-action pairs: uncertainty associated with what the learner has not yet established. The authors connect this construction theoretically to LSVI-UCB in the linear setting, grounding the proposed deep-learning method in an existing exploration framework.

The method also updates episodes backward so that uncertainty about future outcomes propagates in a time-consistent way. This component empirically improves sample efficiency. Experiments in MNIST maze and Atari suggest that the complete method outperforms several state-of-the-art exploration approaches, supporting the combination of bootstrap uncertainty estimates with coordinated backward updates.
icml-2021-principled-exploration-via-opt.tldr: Bootstrap uncertainty bonuses and backward episodic updates provide a principled exploration method with promising deep reinforcement-learning results.

paragraphs: Online allocation requires making decisions as requests arrive, with each action earning a reward and consuming limited resources. The paper extends this setup by adding a nonlinear regularizer that depends on total resource consumption. The objective therefore accounts for both accumulated reward and a preference about how resources are allocated overall.

Internet advertising motivates the formulation. An allocation system may seek revenue or efficiency while also valuing fairness or penalizing under-delivery of advertisements. Encoding these concerns through the regularizer makes them part of the optimization objective, alongside the requirement to respect resource limits throughout the allocation problem.

The authors design a simple, fast algorithm for requests drawn independently from an unknown distribution. It achieves the optimal order of sublinear regret relative to an allocation chosen with hindsight, so its shortfall grows more slowly than the horizon. Numerical advertising experiments confirm the effectiveness of both the algorithm and the regularizers under study, connecting the formulation to its motivating application.
icml-2021-regularized-online-allocation-.tldr: A regularized online-allocation framework incorporates fairness or delivery goals and achieves optimal-order sublinear regret under independent arrivals.

paragraphs: A policy learned using a simulator may face different conditions in the real world because the simulator’s parameters are uncertain or inaccurate. This paper studies that problem through robust Markov decision processes, whose goal is to find policies that withstand such uncertainty. It focuses on model-free reinforcement learning with large state spaces.

The first contribution is Robust Least Squares Policy Evaluation, an online, multistep method for evaluating a policy. The authors prove that this evaluation algorithm converges using stochastic approximation techniques. Policy evaluation is a building block here: it supplies the assessment needed before policy improvement can be considered.

The paper then introduces Robust Least Squares Policy Iteration to learn a robust policy and provides a weighted Euclidean-norm bound on the resulting policy’s distance from optimality. This gives a quantitative theoretical characterization of policy error. Demonstrations on OpenAI Gym benchmark problems complement the convergence and performance analysis, showing the proposed iteration method operating on practical reinforcement-learning tasks.
icml-2021-robust-reinforcement-learning-.tldr: Robust least-squares policy evaluation and iteration address uncertain dynamics with convergence and policy-error guarantees.

paragraphs: Deep Skill Graphs gives an agent a discrete planning structure for an environment with a large, continuous state space. The graph’s nodes represent skill subgoals, and its edges represent policies that carry out skills. This turns acquired behaviors into components the agent can use when planning how to move through the environment.

During unsupervised training, the agent alternates between discovering skills and planning with the skills already available. These activities support one another: the current graph guides exploration, and newly discovered skills help extend coverage to larger portions of the state space. The graph is built through this ongoing interaction.

When given a new goal at test time, the agent first plans through the learned graph to reach a nearby state, then learns how to reach the goal itself. On four difficult continuous-control tasks, the method outperforms both flat and existing hierarchical reinforcement-learning approaches. The results support combining reusable skills, structured planning, and final goal-specific learning.
icml-2021-skill-discovery-for-exploratio.tldr: Deep Skill Graphs interleaves skill discovery and planning to expand exploration and help an agent reach new goals.

paragraphs: Deep equilibrium networks replace an explicit stack of layers with the fixed point of a nonlinear update: a representation that stops changing under that update. They can offer strong predictive performance with much lower memory use, but their computation can be slow and unstable, with sensitivity to architectural choices.

The paper proposes regularizing the Jacobian of the fixed-point equations, which describes how the update responds to changes in its inputs. This directly targets the behavior of the equilibrium computation. The authors show that the added computational cost is minimal and that convergence becomes substantially more stable in both forward and backward passes.

The approach scales to WikiText-103 language modeling and ImageNet classification. It enables an implicit-depth model with approximately the speed and performance of conventional networks such as ResNet-101, while preserving the constant memory footprint and architectural simplicity associated with DEQs. The result links a stability-focused regularizer to improved practical competitiveness for equilibrium-based networks.
icml-2021-stabilizing-equilibrium-models.tldr: Jacobian regularization stabilizes equilibrium networks and enables conventional-network-like speed and performance while preserving their memory advantages.

paragraphs: Quantized neural networks restrict their weights, making them relevant to energy efficiency, inference speed, and hardware deployment. Finding optimal weights under those restrictions introduces combinatorial, nonconvex optimization problems. This paper investigates whether some of these training problems can instead be handled through a convex optimization formulation.

The proposed strategy applies to networks with polynomial activations. It combines hidden convexity in two-layer networks with semidefinite lifting and Grothendieck’s identity. These mathematical tools allow the authors to formulate semidefinite relaxations and analyze when those relaxations recover the original optimization problem exactly.

For certain quantized-network problems, the relaxations are tight, yielding provable global optimality in time polynomial in all relevant parameters. The qualification matters: the result establishes tractability for the identified problems within the studied network setting. Numerical examples illustrate the method’s effectiveness. The main contribution is a constructive route from a seemingly intractable discrete training problem to a convex program with an exact optimality guarantee in those cases.
icml-2021-training-quantized-neural-netw.tldr: Tight semidefinite relaxations solve certain quantized neural-network training problems to global optimality in polynomial time.

paragraphs: Learning an energy-based latent-variable model can require its score function and the score’s gradient with respect to model parameters. The paper expresses these quantities through expectations and covariances over the posterior distribution of latent variables. That posterior is generally intractable, making the needed calculations difficult to perform directly.

The authors introduce estimates that replace the true posterior in those expressions with a variational approximation. They train this approximation by minimizing a divergence from the true posterior, such as KL divergence. Their theory connects that divergence to upper bounds on estimation bias, giving a mathematical relationship between posterior approximation quality and the accuracy of the resulting estimates.

In principle, the estimates support several objectives, including kernelized Stein discrepancy, score-matching methods, and exact Fisher divergence under a minimal model assumption. Applied specifically to score-matching methods, they outperform existing approaches for learning energy-based latent-variable models on several image datasets. The empirical result supports that application, while the broader objective coverage is a stated potential use.
icml-2021-variational-gradient-estimate-.tldr: Variational posterior approximations yield score and gradient estimates with bias bounds and improved score-matching results for energy-based latent-variable models.
